title: How Skywriting Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain skywriting: how freehand skywriting works with paraffin oil smoke released from planes, its origins with WWI aviator John Clifford Savage, its use in advertising (Captain Cyril Turner, Pepsi, Lucky Strike), why television displaced it, the rarity of skilled skywriters, and the newer digital skytyping method using multiple planes. They also cover Kurt Braunohler's "How do I land?" stunt, John Lennon and Yoko Ono's "War is over" message, a Microsoft fake-skywriting patent, and a listener mail about vulture vomit and a skunk spray story.

segments.title: Origins and early military use of skywriting
segments.summary: Skywriting is traced to WWI-era flying aces and John Clifford Savage, with early military uses for messaging beyond radio range and possibly cloaking ships in smoke.

segments.title: Skywriting goes commercial: Captain Cyril Turner and early ads
segments.summary: Captain Cyril Turner wrote the first skywritten advertisement, for the Daily Mail, then Hello USA over Times Square and a phone number that drew 47,000 calls. Companies such as Lucky Strike, Snocco and Pepsi adopted it heavily.

segments.title: Decline of skywriting and the rise of television ads
segments.summary: Skywriting faded as television advertising offered better targeting and reach, and skywriting depends on clear, calm weather. The New York Times had predicted celestial vandalism that never fully materialized.
topics: The Atlantic What Happened to Skywriting

segments.title: How freehand skywriting is performed
segments.summary: Skywriting is done at about 10,000 feet using paraffin oil smoke from high-horsepower planes flying about 150 mph. Pilots write backwards, use ground references and timing, and the Pepsi word takes many maneuvers. Few skilled practitioners remain, including Suzanne Asbury Oliver and Steve Oliver, and the skill is passed on by apprenticeship.

segments.title: Digital skytyping with multiple planes
segments.summary: Skytyping, invented by Andy Stinnes in the 1940s, uses at least five planes flying in formation and releasing puffs of smoke controlled by computer, producing neater dot-matrix-like messages. Costs are much higher than freehand skywriting, and the Pie in the Sky message in Austin is cited as an example.

segments.title: Famous skywritten messages, costs, and social media revival
segments.summary: Examples include John Lennon and Yoko Ono's War is over message over Toronto, costs from around fifty dollars up to about six thousand eight hundred for Braunohler's message, a Microsoft patent for faking skywriting in photos, and social media helping skywriting's revival.
